# Spring water

Spring water emerges from the ground where the saturated zone of an aquifer meets the surface. The discharge can be a trickle or a torrent, depending on the size of the aquifer and the porosity of the rock above it.

Geologists distinguish gravity springs, which surface where the water table intersects the land, from artesian springs, which are pushed upward through fractures by hydrostatic pressure. Both are sensitive to seasonal recharge and to land use changes upslope.

In many regions, springs were the first reliable sources of drinking water and shaped the placement of early settlements. Today they remain useful indicators of groundwater health: when a spring runs dry or muddy, the surrounding aquifer is almost always in trouble.
